newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's UES to tap markets as it restructures.
newsitem.headline: Russia's UES to tap markets as it restructures.

text.p: Russian stock market star Unified Energy System (UES) announced on Thursday ambitious plans to issue securities abroad as it takes painful steps to restructure the domestic electricity sector which it controls.
UES's 29-year old boss Boris Brevnov told Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin at a government meeting he was ready to reform Russia's largest company without state support.
"He said it was the first time he did not hear a request for budget support," Brevnov told a news conference.
But the federal government will ante up 2.7 percent of UES stock, twice the commitment earlier publicised, in a convertible bond programme to begin by autumn, Brevnov said.
Russian news agencies quoted him as telling the meeting UES would raise about $1.25 billion from the progamme, though it was not clear what part of the proceeds would go to the government.
UES owns the national electric grid, has controlling stakes in almost every regional power utility and has its own generating power as well.
Its shares gained almost 10 percent to close on the Russian Trading System at $0.447, about five times its price at the beginning of the year.

It is the market volume leader and plans to begin an American Despositary Receipts programme to allow foreign trade of its shares this summer. Brevnov said shares were still undervalued by a factor of 10.
But the company is mired in a non-payments crisis, supporting large parts of Russian industry and branches of the government itself which are not able to pay for their energy.
Brevnov said he and the government had made some progress towards solving non-payment and cash flow problems.
"If they lost half their turnover and got the cash in the system up to 50 percent from 20 percent that would be an enormous net gain," said United City Bank research director Christopher Granville.
UES will cancel debts it is owed at the same time it pays what it owes, Brevnov said, adding that UES would also begin to take short-term promissory notes as payment.

The company this week also began an ambitious experiment to open a wholesale power market, which would allow major clients to buy directly from power generators and receive discounts of up to 30 percent for cash payments.

Such moves could be oil to the creaking financial machinery of UES. Brevnov and First Deputy Fuel and Energy Minister Sergei Kiriyenko said the government would attempt to begin paying for current electricity use and restructure payment backlogs.
Brevnov said a list of protected users which are guaranteed power despite non-payments would have to be whittled down, and Kiriyenko said enterprises should learn to live by their means.
"It is not a question of cutting off (non-payers)," he said. "The government's job is to figure out how much energy it can pay for."

UES has successfully kept control of the generating and transmitting parts of its operations, but Brevnov may be aiming to increase UES's size by taking over one of the most prominent independent regional utilities, Irkutskenergo IRGZ.RTS.
"Brevnov said UES is holding talks at the moment with Siberian company Irkutskenergo on incorporating it into a single energy system," Interfax news agency reported from the government meeting.
Irkutskenergo, one of the few regional producers with an excess of energy, wants to export electricity to near-by Mongolia without interference from UES.
